content: 1. Recommendations from previous guidelines, which were approved by the review committee, have been updated after a thorough review of evidence and discussions within the Guideline Development Group (GDG). These updates include clarifications and new recommendations specific to the current guidelines. 2. Not all individuals infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis develop active tuberculosis (TB). The lifetime risk of progression from latent TB infection (LTBI) to active TB is estimated to be 5–10%. This risk is particularly elevated in children under 5 years of age and individuals with compromised immune systems. 3. Preventive treatment for M. tuberculosis infection carries inherent risks and costs. Therefore, it should be selectively targeted toward population groups at the highest risk of progression to active TB, as these individuals are most likely to benefit from LTBI treatment. 4. When selecting at-risk populations for programmatic management of LTBI, the epidemiology and transmission patterns of TB in the specific country should be considered to ensure that treatment provides long-lasting protection. 5. A comprehensive individual clinical assessment is a critical component of programmatic management. This assessment should carefully weigh the risks and benefits of treatment for each individual. 6. Adults and adolescents living with HIV, regardless of their immune status or whether they are on antiretroviral therapy (ART), should receive preventive TB treatment as part of a comprehensive HIV care package. This includes individuals with unknown or positive tuberculin skin test (TST) results, those previously treated for TB, and pregnant women. This recommendation is strongly supported by high-quality evidence. 7. TB remains the leading cause of AIDS-related deaths globally, despite advancements in ART access. In 2016, TB caused approximately 400,000 deaths among people living with HIV, accounting for one-third of all HIV-related deaths. 8. Observational studies and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have demonstrated the efficacy of preventive TB treatment in individuals receiving ART. For example, a double-blind RCT involving 1,329 people living with HIV on ART showed that those with negative TST or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) results benefited more from isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) than those with positive results. 9. Preventive treatment combined with ART has been shown to reduce TB incidence and overall mortality, with protective effects lasting for more than five years. 10. Infants under 12 months of age living with HIV who have been in contact with a TB case and are found not to have active TB should receive six months of IPT. This recommendation is based on moderate-quality evidence and has been updated in the current guidelines. 11. Children aged 12 months or older living with HIV, who are unlikely to have active TB based on symptom screening and have no known TB contact, should be offered six months of IPT if they live in settings with a high prevalence of TB. This recommendation is strongly supported by low-quality evidence. 12. All children living with HIV who have successfully completed treatment for TB disease may receive an additional six months of isoniazid. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 13. Preventive treatment is recommended for children living with HIV who are exposed to reinfection or recurrence of TB, particularly in high TB incidence settings. Preventive treatment can be initiated immediately after completing TB therapy or later, depending on clinical judgment. 14. HIV-negative children under 5 years of age who are household contacts of individuals with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB and are found not to have active TB should receive TB preventive treatment. This recommendation is strongly supported by high-quality evidence. 15. In countries with low TB incidence, systematic testing and treatment for LTBI should be conducted for adults, adolescents, and children who are household contacts of individuals with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB. 16. In high TB incidence settings, children aged 5 years or older, adolescents, and adults who are household contacts of individuals with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB and are found not to have active TB may be given TB preventive treatment. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 17. Patients initiating anti-TNF treatment, those receiving dialysis, those preparing for organ or hematological transplants, and those with silicosis should be systematically tested and treated for LTBI. This recommendation is strongly supported by low to very low-quality evidence. 18. In low TB incidence countries, systematic testing and treatment for LTBI may be considered for prisoners, healthcare workers, immigrants from high TB burden countries, homeless individuals, and people who use illicit drugs. This is a conditional recommendation based on low to very low-quality evidence. 19. Systematic testing for LTBI is not recommended for individuals with diabetes, harmful alcohol use, tobacco use, or underweight status unless they are already included in the above recommendations. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 20. Testing and treatment for LTBI should adhere strictly to human rights and ethical considerations. For example, positive test results or LTBI treatment should not affect a person’s immigration status or delay their ability to immigrate. 21. The GDG reviewed evidence from systematic reviews to identify at-risk population groups for LTBI testing and treatment. Evidence of increased LTBI prevalence, progression to active TB, and active TB incidence was found for 15 risk groups, including TB contacts, healthcare workers, people living with HIV, dialysis patients, immigrants from high TB burden countries, and others. 22. Infants and young children under 5 years of age are at significantly higher risk of developing active TB, which can progress rapidly and lead to severe and disseminated disease with high morbidity and mortality. Therefore, preventive treatment is strongly recommended for child household contacts under 5 years of age, provided active TB disease has been ruled out. 23. Preventive treatment may also be considered conditionally for household contacts in other age groups, depending on clinical judgment, the balance of harm and benefit, and the local TB epidemiology. 24. The availability of resources and the capacity of the healthcare infrastructure to assess exposure risk, weigh harm and benefit, and exclude active TB disease before initiating treatment are important considerations in the conditionality of these recommendations.
